docs.title: Vortex V1 HAL
docs.text:
The software layer for the HardFOC Vortex V1 motor controller board. One Vortex object gives your ESP32-C6 application the TMC9660 motor controller, encoders, the IMU, temperatures, ADC channels, GPIO, CAN, storage and a status LED, through a small set of managers that know the board's wiring.

Get started See the architecture

docs.title: What the board is
docs.text:
Vortex V1 drives one motor. An ESP32-C6 runs your application and talks to a TMC9660, a motor controller with integrated gate drivers and its own current, velocity and position loops (BLDC, stepper or brushed DC), over UART (the default) or SPI. Around it sit an AS5047U magnetic angle encoder slot on SPI, a BNO08x IMU and a PCAL95555 I/O expander on I2C, an NTC thermistor read through the TMC9660, a CAN port and a WS2812 status LED. The hardware page shows every bus and pin.

This repository (hf-hal-vortex-v1) is the hardware abstraction layer (HAL): it turns that board into C++ objects. Your application does not touch GPIO numbers or SPI frames; it calls vortex.motors, vortex.encoders, vortex.temp.

Figure description and sources

From top to bottom, each layer only calls the one under it. Your application asks the facade singleton for the managers. The managers (one per board function) own the hf-core handlers, which wrap one chip driver each; a manager may also use a driver directly. Drivers talk to hardware only through the interface classes of the internal interface wrap, whose ESP32 implementations sit on ESP-IDF. Every name in a band is read from the code: the managers from the facade's member references, the handlers, drivers and interface classes from the managers' and handlers' #include lines.

Drawn from: lib/api/Vortex.h Vortex (manager references); lib/managers #includes; lib/core/handlers #includes; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/hal-layers.py.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from nothing to a Vortex V1 board printing its start-up log. Each step says how to tell that it worked. Plan on half an hour, most of it the ESP-IDF download.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Item Notes A Vortex V1 board The board starts and logs over USB alone USB cable Data-capable; the ESP32-C6 enumerates as a USB serial / JTAG device A motor supply Only to spin a motor. Without it the motor manager comes up degraded, which is expected Linux, macOS or Windows (WSL2) The build scripts are Bash

docs.title: 1. Install ESP-IDF
docs.text:
The examples target esp32c6 and build with ESP-IDF release/v5.5 (both read from examples/esp32/app_config.yml, which CI uses too).

mkdir -p ~/esp && cd ~/esp
git clone -b release/v5.5 --recursive https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf.git
cd esp-idf && ./install.sh esp32c6
. ./export.sh

It worked if idf.py --version prints a v5.5 version. Run . ~/esp/esp-idf/export.sh in every new terminal.

docs.title: 2. Clone with submodules
docs.text:
The HAL pulls the shared core (lib/core: handlers, drivers, the pin map), the build scripts and CANopenNode as git submodules.

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-hal-vortex-v1.git
cd hf-hal-vortex-v1

If you already cloned without submodules:

git submodule update --init --recursive

It worked if ls lib/core/handlers lists handler folders and ls examples/esp32/scripts shows build_app.sh.

One submodule is private

docs/hf-development-handbook is a private repository and is marked update = none, so the recursive update skips it. You do not need it to build.

docs.title: 3. Build an example
docs.text:
Every example is an "app" selected by name. Start with vortex_api_test, the default app, which initialises the whole HAL and exercises each manager.

cd examples/esp32
./scripts/build_app.sh list                        # every app name
./scripts/build_app.sh vortex_api_test Release     # build one

It worked if the script ends with a successful link and a build folder named after the app, the build type and the target appears under examples/esp32/.

docs.title: 4. Flash and monitor
docs.text:
Connect the board over USB, then:

./scripts/flash_app.sh flash_monitor vortex_api_test Release

Set ESPPORT first if more than one serial port is present (for example export ESPPORT=/dev/ttyACM0). Leave the monitor with Ctrl+].

It worked if the log shows Vortex API initialization completed successfully in ... ms followed by a Component Status line with OK or FAIL for each of NVS, Comms, GPIO, Motors, ADC, IMU, Encoders, LEDs and Temp. FAIL on Motors, ADC or Temp without a motor supply is normal: those steps are best effort. See Initialisation.

docs.title: 5. Use the HAL in your own code
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/LedManager.h"
#include "managers/TemperatureManager.h"

extern "C" void app_main() {
    auto& vortex = Vortex::GetInstance();
    if (!vortex.EnsureInitialized()) {
        return;  // NVS, comms, GPIO or the LED failed: nothing below can work
    }
    (void)vortex.leds.IndicateReady();

    float chip_c = 0.0f;
    if (vortex.temp.ReadInternalTemperature(chip_c) == hf_temp_err_t::TEMP_SUCCESS) {
        // chip_c is the ESP32-C6 die temperature
    }
}

The next large piece of work is making Vortex V1 a CiA 402 servo drive node on its CAN port: one object dictionary as the single source for firmware, EDS file and tools; CANopenNode v4 behind a narrow stack interface; the TMC9660's own loops doing the motion while the ESP32-C6 runs the CiA 402 state machine, limits and faults; and host tests that run the same node against a simulated motor.

docs.title: ADR 0001: Keep the MCU behind the interface wrap; only managers know the board
docs.text: Status Accepted (records the current design) Date 2026-11-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: HardFOC boards share chips (the TMC9660, AS5047U, BNO08x, WS2812, CAN) and a common core (hf-core: handlers, drivers, interface wrap). Vortex V1 runs on an ESP32-C6 today. A future Vortex is expected on an STM32 with CAN FD, and the CANopen device work planned for the board is meant to move with it unchanged. The motor, sensor and protocol code must not be tied to ESP-IDF.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Write the HAL directly against ESP-IDF. Fast to start; every manager and handler would need rewriting for another MCU.
  2. Put the MCU behind interface classes and keep board knowledge in one layer. Chip drivers and handlers use only BaseSpi, BaseI2c, BaseGpio, BaseAdc, BaseCan, BaseUart, BaseNvs, BaseTemperature; the managers are the only code that knows which chip is on which pin of which board.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Option 2. The boundary is:

  • Drivers and handlers (in hf-core) depend only on the Base* interface classes.
  • The ESP32 implementations (EspSpiBus, EspI2cBus, EspUart, EspCan, EspGpio, EspNvs, EspTemperature) are named only in the managers that create buses and peripherals: CommChannelsManager, GpioManager, NvsManager and TemperatureManager. The generated manager map lists every manager's interface classes, read from the #include lines.
  • Board wiring lives in the per-board pin map in hf-pincfg (ADR 0003).
  • Application code sees managers, handlers and Base* pointers (for example BaseCan* from GetCanOpenBus()), never Esp* types.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A port to another MCU replaces the Esp* construction in those four managers with another implementation of the same interfaces (the Stm* classes in the interface wrap are the start of one) and adds a pin map; handlers, drivers and code above the managers stay.
  • CAN FD fits the same seam: an FD-capable BaseCan implementation (frames up to 64 bytes, data-phase bit timing) is created by CommChannelsManager instead of EspCan. Code that only sees BaseCan* keeps working; code that wants FD frames checks the port's capabilities. BaseCan's message type still carries 8 data bytes, so enlarging it is the first step of an FD port.
  • Known leaks across the boundary today, to fix before a port: LedManager uses the ESP-IDF RMT WS2812 driver and returns a gpio_num_t; CommChannelsManager.cpp writes ESP32 port numbers (SPI host 1, I2C_NUM_0, UART port 1); examples/esp32 call ESP-IDF directly, which is fine for examples.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Allocate once at start-up; fixed tables, no growing containers
docs.text: Status Accepted (records the current design, with the exceptions listed) Date 2026-11-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The board drives a motor for long periods. Heap fragmentation or an allocation failure in the middle of a control loop is hard to diagnose and can leave the drive in an unknown state. On the other hand, which chips answer is only known at start-up, external devices are added by the application, and some objects (bus drivers, chip drivers) are easiest to create on the heap. The examples build with C++ exceptions off.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Everything static. No heap at all; every driver object a member. Rigid, and some driver classes are not designed for it.
  2. Allocate during start-up and device creation, never in a read, write or control call. Tables with a known size are fixed arrays; objects whose existence depends on start-up results are created on the heap and kept for the program's life.
  3. Allocate freely. Simple, and the problems above.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Option 2:

  • Tables are std::array sized at compile time: the GPIO and ADC entries (from the pin map), the SPI device table (SpiDeviceId::DEVICE_COUNT), the handler slots (MAX_TMC9660_DEVICES, MAX_IMU_DEVICES, MAX_ENCODER_DEVICES, all 4), the bounded runtime I2C slots, and the facade's diagnostics arrays (kVortexManagerCount).
  • Bus objects, handlers and drivers are held in std::unique_ptr (GPIO pins in std::shared_ptr, because their owners differ), created when the owning manager initialises or when you create a device.
  • No manager allocates in its read, write, motion or LED calls.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• After Vortex::EnsureInitialized(), and once your own devices are created, the motor, ADC, temperature, GPIO, encoder, IMU and LED paths do not touch the heap.

Where this is not strictly true today:

  • Run-time device creation allocates: CreateI2cDevice(), MotorController::CreateExternalDevice(), ImuManager::CreateExternalBno08xDevice(), EncoderManager::CreateAs5047uDevice(). Create devices during your own start-up.
  • Most managers use std::make_unique / std::make_shared; with exceptions off, an allocation failure aborts instead of failing initialisation. Only TemperatureManager uses hf::utils::make_unique_nothrow.
  • ImuManager::ConfigureInterrupt() stores a std::function, which may allocate for a capturing callback.
  • Allocations inside ESP-IDF and the chip drivers are not covered by this decision.

docs.title: ADR 0003: The hf-pincfg X-macro table is the single source of pin truth
docs.text: Status Accepted (records the current design) Date 2026-11-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A pin number written in more than one place drifts: the schematic changes, one copy is updated, another is not, and the board misbehaves in a way no compiler catches. Vortex V1 spreads its pins over three chips (ESP32-C6, PCAL95555, TMC9660), which makes copies even easier to get wrong. Pin numbers used to be repeated in this repository's README and docs.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Pins as constants in each manager. Simple; every manager and every document repeats them.
  2. One table per board, used by the code and by the docs. The board's functional pin map in hf-pincfg (hf_functional_pin_config_vortex_v1.hpp), written as X-macro rows; everything else reads it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Option 2:

  • Each row of HF_FUNCTIONAL_GPIO_PIN_LIST / HF_FUNCTIONAL_ADC_CHANNEL_LIST names a function, its chip, unit, pin, polarity, pull, drive and current. The same rows generate the enums, name tables and mapping arrays.
  • The managers register from the generated arrays: GpioManager creates a pin for each GPIO-category row on whichever chip it is, AdcManager a channel for each ADC row; CommChannelsManager and the facade look pins up by HfFunctionalGpioPin (GetGpioMapping(), gpio.Get(...)). No manager writes a GPIO number.
  • The pin map page and the board figure are generated from the same rows (tools/docs/gen.py, tools/figkit/build.py), and CI fails if they are stale.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Changing a pin is one edit in hf-pincfg, a submodule bump here, and a docs rebuild.
  • The pin map is shared by every HardFOC HAL through hf-pincfg; the board is chosen at build time with HARDFOC_BOARD_VORTEX_V1 (set in this repository's CMakeLists.txt).
  • One copy remains: vortex_board_pins.hpp repeats the bus and LED GPIO numbers for examples that call ESP-IDF directly. It says it must match the pin map but nothing checks it; a compile-time check against the pin map would close the gap.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
How the Vortex V1 HAL is put together. The short version: your code talks to one object, Vortex; Vortex holds one manager per board function; managers own hf-core handlers; handlers wrap chip drivers; drivers reach the hardware only through the interface classes of the internal interface wrap, which sit on ESP-IDF.

Figure description and sources

From top to bottom, each layer only calls the one under it. Your application asks the facade singleton for the managers. The managers (one per board function) own the hf-core handlers, which wrap one chip driver each; a manager may also use a driver directly. Drivers talk to hardware only through the interface classes of the internal interface wrap, whose ESP32 implementations sit on ESP-IDF. Every name in a band is read from the code: the managers from the facade's member references, the handlers, drivers and interface classes from the managers' and handlers' #include lines.

Drawn from: lib/api/Vortex.h Vortex (manager references); lib/managers #includes; lib/core/handlers #includes; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/hal-layers.py.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
Layer Where What it does You use it when Application your project, examples/esp32 Tasks, control loops, protocols Always Facade lib/api/Vortex.h One singleton; brings the managers up in order; system diagnostics Always: Vortex::GetInstance() Managers lib/managers One per board function (motors, encoders, IMU, ADC, ...); know the board's wiring from the pin map Almost always: vortex.motors, vortex.encoders, ... hf-core handlers lib/core/handlers Wrap one chip driver each and adapt it to the interface classes Rarely; for chip features a manager does not expose Chip drivers lib/core/hf-core-drivers/external Register-level drivers, one repository per chip Almost never from application code Interface wrap lib/core/hf-core-drivers/internal/hf-internal-interface-wrap BaseSpi, BaseGpio, BaseAdc, ... and their ESP32 implementations (EspSpi, EspGpio, ...) When porting to another MCU

The rule that holds the design together: a layer only calls the layer below it. The managers are the only code that knows Vortex V1 exists; handlers and drivers are shared with other HardFOC boards. Why the line is drawn there is recorded in ADR 0001.

docs.title: Errors and diagnostics
docs.text: The HAL does not throw: the examples build with C++ exceptions off, every call is noexcept and failure comes back in the return value. This page lists the error types, where to read the last error, and the system diagnostics.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
1. Check the return value. Most methods are [[nodiscard]]; the compiler warns if you drop a result.
  2. A method that returns bool returns false on failure; a method that returns a pointer returns nullptr when the manager is not initialised or the thing you asked for does not exist.
  3. Every manager has GetLastError(). Prefer the value a call returns: the last error is shared by every caller of that manager and may already describe a later call.

docs.title: Error types by manager
docs.text:
Manager Error type To text NvsManager hf_nvs_err_t (set on initialisation) HfNvsErrToString() CommChannelsManager CommError CommErrorToString() GpioManager hf_gpio_err_t HfGpioErrToString() MotorController MotorError MotorErrorToString() AdcManager hf_adc_err_t HfAdcErrToString() ImuManager ImuError ImuErrorToString() EncoderManager EncoderError EncoderErrorToString() LedManager LedError LedErrorToString() TemperatureManager hf_temp_err_t HfTempErrToString()

The board-specific enums (CommError, MotorError, ImuError, EncoderError, LedError) start with SUCCESS (0), then NOT_INITIALIZED, then manager-specific values. The hf_*_err_t types come from the interface wrap and are shared with every HardFOC board.

docs.title: System diagnostics
docs.text:
All of these are on the Vortex object. CollectManagerHealth() and PerformHealthCheck() return false until EnsureInitialized() has succeeded.

Call Gives you GetSystemDiagnostics(VortexSystemDiagnostics&) Which managers initialised, how many failed (and their names), start-up time, uptime; system_healthy GetComponentInitializationStatus() std::array<bool, 9>, one flag per manager GetFailedComponents(out, max) Names of managers whose initialisation failed CollectManagerHealth(ManagerHealthSnapshot&) Per manager: initialised, has an error, last error code (as uint8_t), and an overall all_healthy PerformHealthCheck() Logs the health snapshot and returns whether all managers are healthy (false before initialisation) DumpSystemStatistics() Logs every manager's statistics GetSystemUptimeMs(), GetInitializationTimeMs(), GetSystemVersion() Timing and the HAL version string

The last error code in a health entry is the manager's own enum cast to uint8_t; read it with the table above. Each manager also has GetSystemDiagnostics(...) and DumpStatistics(); see the manager pages.

ManagerHealthSnapshot health;
if (Vortex::GetInstance().CollectManagerHealth(health) && !health.all_healthy) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < health.count; ++i) {
        const auto& e = health.entries[i];
        if (!e.initialized || e.has_error) {
            ESP_LOGW("app", "%s: init=%d error=%u", e.name, e.initialized, e.last_error_code);
        }
    }
}

Known gap

GetSystemWarnings() always returns no entries today: the facade has a warning list, but nothing adds to it. Best-effort start-up failures are visible in the log (Initialized in degraded mode ...) and through GetFailedComponents() / GetComponentInitializationStatus().

docs.title: Initialisation
docs.text:
Vortex::EnsureInitialized() brings every manager up, one at a time, in a fixed order. Call it once, early in app_main(), before you touch any manager.

Figure description and sources

Left to right, then the second row. The facade initialises the managers one at a time, in the order of the calls in its init function. The first group is required: if any of them fails, EnsureInitialized() returns false and the application should not continue. The second group is best effort: a failure there is logged as a warning, the manager stays unavailable and the system reports itself as degraded, so a bench with only some chips fitted still comes up. The order and the required / best-effort split are read from the init function, which returns false only in the required branches.

Drawn from: lib/api/Vortex.cpp Vortex::InitializeAllComponents; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/init-order.py.

docs.title: The order
docs.text:
Generated by tools/docs/gen.py from Vortex.cpp (Vortex::InitializeAllComponents); do not edit.

Step Manager Member If it fails 1 NvsManager vortex.nvs initialisation fails (EnsureInitialized() returns false) 2 CommChannelsManager vortex.comms initialisation fails (EnsureInitialized() returns false) 3 GpioManager vortex.gpio initialisation fails (EnsureInitialized() returns false) 4 LedManager vortex.leds initialisation fails (EnsureInitialized() returns false) 5 MotorController vortex.motors warning; the system runs degraded 6 AdcManager vortex.adc warning; the system runs degraded 7 ImuManager vortex.imu warning; the system runs degraded 8 EncoderManager vortex.encoders warning; the system runs degraded 9 TemperatureManager vortex.temp warning; the system runs degraded

The order follows the dependencies: storage first, so configuration and calibration can be read early; then the buses; then the GPIO pins, which include the PCAL95555 expander lines the TMC9660 needs; then the status LED, early so an LED-only bench works without the motor controller. After that come the managers that depend on the TMC9660: AdcManager reads its channels through the TMC9660, and TemperatureManager reads the NTC through AdcManager and the chip temperature from the TMC9660.

docs.title: What happens when a step fails
docs.text:
• Required steps (NVS, comms, GPIO, LEDs). If one fails, EnsureInitialized() logs an error, stops and returns false. IsInitialized() stays false, and calling EnsureInitialized() again retries from the start.
  • Best-effort steps (motors, ADC, IMU, encoders, temperature). A failure is logged as a warning and the manager stays unavailable; the remaining steps still run and EnsureInitialized() returns true. The log then says Initialized in degraded mode and lists which of Motors, ADC, IMU, Enc and Temp are OFF. Check vortex.motors.IsInitialized() (or the diagnostics) before relying on a best-effort manager.

This lets a bench with only some chips fitted, or with the motor supply off, still come up and log.

docs.title: The onboard TMC9660 and its transport
docs.text:
Step 5 creates the onboard TMC9660 before initialising MotorController. It takes the four TMC9660 control lines (reset, driver enable, fault, wake) from GpioManager, which is why GPIO comes first, and registers the chip on one of two host links:

Transport How to select it What happens UART (default) nothing TMCL over the UART at TMCL address 1; the SPI mux pin PCAL_TMC_SPI_COMM_EN stays released SPI Vortex::SetOnboardTmc9660Transport(VortexOnboardTmc9660Transport::Spi) before EnsureInitialized() TMCL over SPI2; MotorController asserts the SPI mux while it talks to the chip

SetOnboardTmc9660Transport() is ignored (with a warning) once initialisation has completed.

docs.title: Calling a manager directly
docs.text: Every manager has its own EnsureInitialized(), which returns true at once if the manager is already up. Code that uses one manager on its own can call it, but going through Vortex::EnsureInitialized() gives the right order, the onboard TMC9660 registration and the system diagnostics. EncoderManager creates no device by itself; see EncoderManager.

docs.title: Shutting down
docs.text: Vortex::Shutdown() de-initialises every initialised manager, in this order: temperature, LEDs, encoders, IMU, ADC, motors, GPIO, comms, NVS. That is the start-up order reversed except for the LED manager, which is shut down second although it starts fourth. It then clears the initialised flag, so a later EnsureInitialized() starts again from the beginning. It returns false if the HAL was not initialised.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Who creates each object, who owns it, and how memory is allocated. The short version: the facade owns nothing but references; each manager is a singleton that owns its handlers and bus objects for the life of the program; other managers borrow them.

Figure description and sources

Managers on the left, hf-core handlers in the middle, chip drivers on the right. An arrow means "includes and uses": a manager owns or borrows the handler it points at, and each handler wraps exactly one driver. Several managers share the TMC9660 handler, because that one chip provides motor control, GPIO, ADC channels and a temperature sensor; MotorController owns it and the others reach it through MotorController. LedManager uses its driver directly, without a handler. Managers with no arrow (communication buses, NVS) talk to the interface wrap only.

Drawn from: lib/managers #includes; lib/core/handlers #includes; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/manager-dependencies.py.

docs.title: Singletons
docs.text: Every manager is a function-local static (GetInstance(), a Meyers singleton): it is constructed on first use and never destroyed. Vortex itself is one, and its members (vortex.comms, vortex.motors, ...) are references to the manager singletons, bound in its constructor. So vortex.motors and MotorController::GetInstance() are the same object; prefer the facade in application code so the start-up order is respected.

docs.title: Who owns what
docs.text:

Borrowed pointers and references stay valid until the owning manager is de-initialised (Vortex::Shutdown() or the manager's own Deinitialize()). Do not keep them across a shutdown.

docs.title: GPIO pins have three owners
docs.text:
GpioManager stores every pin as a std::shared_ptr<BaseGpio>, because the pins come from three places:

  • ESP32 pins: GpioManager creates an EspGpio and owns it.
  • PCAL95555 pins: the expander handler creates the pin object; the shared pointer keeps it alive.
  • TMC9660 pins (TMC_GPIO17, TMC_GPIO18): the TMC9660 handler owns them; GpioManager holds a non-owning shared pointer, registered by RegisterTmc9660BridgePinsIfNeeded() once the onboard handler exists.

docs.title: Allocation
docs.text: Device tables are fixed-size arrays sized at compile time (from the pin map or a MAX_*_DEVICES constant), so there are no growing containers. The objects in those tables (buses, handlers, drivers, pin objects) are created on the heap during initialisation with std::make_unique / std::make_shared and live as long as the manager. After start-up, the heap is used again only when you create or delete a device at run time: CreateI2cDevice(), MotorController::CreateExternalDevice(), ImuManager::CreateExternalBno08xDevice(), EncoderManager::CreateAs5047uDevice(). ADR 0002 records this rule and where the code does not yet meet it.

docs.title: Threading
docs.text: What you can safely call from more than one FreeRTOS task. The HAL creates no tasks of its own: every call runs in the task that makes it. Periodic work, such as LED animation steps, is driven by your code.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
Each manager (except NvsManager) has one RtosMutex from hf-utils-rtos-wrap. EnsureInitialized() uses a double-checked pattern: an atomic "initialised" flag is read first, then the lock is taken and the flag checked again.

Manager Locked operations Not locked CommChannelsManager EnsureInitialized(), GetSystemDiagnostics(), Deinitialize() Bus and device accessors (GetSpiDevice(), GetI2cDevice(), GetUartBus(), GetCanBus()) and the runtime I2C calls (CreateI2cDevice(), I2cProbeAddress(), I2cScanBus(), RemoveI2cDevice(), I2cResetBus()) NvsManager none everything; the BaseNvs namespaces do their own work GpioManager EnsureInitialized(), Deinitialize(), GetSystemDiagnostics(), TMC9660 bridge registration every per-pin call (Set(), Read(), Toggle(), SetDirection(), ...) MotorController device creation and deletion, handler(), diagnostics, motor mechanics, load-frame velocity and position setMotorVelocity() / getMotorVelocity() / setMotorPosition() / getMotorPosition() themselves (they go through the handler) AdcManager EnsureInitialized(), Deinitialize(), ReadVoltage(), ReadRaw() Get(), Contains(), Size() ImuManager device creation and lookup, interrupt enable / disable, diagnostics WaitForInterrupt(), GetSensor() EncoderManager device creation and lookup, ReadAllAngles(), ReadAllVelocities(), CheckAllDevicesHealth() single-device reads (ReadAngle(), ReadAngleDegrees(), ReadVelocityRPM(), ReadDiagnostics()) and SetZeroPosition() TemperatureManager EnsureInitialized(), Deinitialize(), ReadTemperatureCelsius() the convenience reads call ReadTemperatureCelsius(), so they are serialised too LedManager colour, brightness and animation calls DumpStatistics() Vortex facade none EnsureInitialized(), Shutdown(); diagnostics read atomics

docs.title: What that means for your code
docs.text:
1. Initialise from one task. Vortex::EnsureInitialized() has no lock of its own: call it once from app_main() before you start other tasks. The same holds for Shutdown().
  2. ADC, temperature, LED and motor configuration calls may be made from several tasks; the manager serialises them. A call can block while another task holds the lock (for example during an SPI or UART transfer).
  3. GPIO: give each pin one owner task, or add your own lock. Two tasks driving the same pin through GpioManager are not serialised, and the operation counters are plain integers.
  4. SPI2 is shared by the TMC9660 (when on SPI), the AS5047U and the external slots. Keep each device to one task, and remember the TMC9660 SPI mux: while it is selected, the TMC9660 sees the SPI2 traffic.
  5. Encoder reads of one device from several tasks: add your own lock, or read all devices with ReadAllAngles(), which takes the manager lock.
  6. LED animations advance only when you call vortex.leds.UpdateAnimation(); call it from a periodic task about every 50 ms.

docs.title: Stack size
docs.text: Vortex::EnsureInitialized() brings up the TMC9660 bootloader, the BNO08x SH-2 stack and the sensors with deep call chains. The examples set CONFIG_ESP_MAIN_TASK_STACK_SIZE=8192 in sdkconfig.defaults; keep at least that much if you initialise from app_main().

docs.title: Vortex V1 HAL, layer by layer
docs.text:
Figure description and sources

From top to bottom, each layer only calls the one under it. Your application asks the facade singleton for the managers. The managers (one per board function) own the hf-core handlers, which wrap one chip driver each; a manager may also use a driver directly. Drivers talk to hardware only through the interface classes of the internal interface wrap, whose ESP32 implementations sit on ESP-IDF. Every name in a band is read from the code: the managers from the facade's member references, the handlers, drivers and interface classes from the managers' and handlers' #include lines.

docs.title: Vortex::EnsureInitialized()
docs.text:
Figure description and sources

Left to right, then the second row. The facade initialises the managers one at a time, in the order of the calls in its init function. The first group is required: if any of them fails, EnsureInitialized() returns false and the application should not continue. The second group is best effort: a failure there is logged as a warning, the manager stays unavailable and the system reports itself as degraded, so a bench with only some chips fitted still comes up. The order and the required / best-effort split are read from the init function, which returns false only in the required branches.

docs.title: Write a page
docs.text:
• Say what the page is for in its first sentence, then answer it. Prefer short sections, tables and numbered steps.
  • Link to code with a relative path, as GitHub resolves it (../../lib/api/Foo.h); the site rewrites the link to the file on GitHub at the commit that was built.
  • Link to the API reference under api/ (../reference/api.md explains it); the link is checked on the built site, after the API is merged.
  • Use admonitions (!!! note, !!! warning) for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration.
  • A new folder gets an index.md; docs/.nav.yml orders the top tabs.

docs.title: Things to know before you wire anything
docs.text:
• The TMC9660 has two host links. The UART is always connected. SPI2 reaches the TMC9660 only while the expander pin PCAL_TMC_SPI_COMM_EN (active low) selects it, because the same SPI2 lines also serve the AS5047U and the external slots. The HAL uses the UART unless you call Vortex::SetOnboardTmc9660Transport(VortexOnboardTmc9660Transport::Spi) before EnsureInitialized().
  • TMC9660 GPIO17 and GPIO18 appear twice in the pin map: as expander inputs (PCAL_TMC_GPIO17_EXP_IN, PCAL_TMC_GPIO18_EXP_IN) and as TMC9660 GPIOs (TMC_GPIO17, TMC_GPIO18). Both views see the same nets.
  • There is no encoder fitted by default. The AS5047U chip select is wired, but EncoderManager creates no device until you call CreateAs5047uDevice().
  • Do not copy pin numbers from TMC9660 evaluation-kit examples. Use the pin map.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
A guided path for a newcomer. Read the pages in this order; each one builds on the one before, and each takes a few minutes.

Step Page You will know 1 Home What Vortex V1 is and what this repository does 2 Get started How to build, flash and read the start-up log 3 Hardware Which chips are on which bus, and the pin map 4 Architecture The layers: facade, managers, handlers, drivers, interface wrap 5 Initialisation What EnsureInitialized() does, in which order, and what can fail 6 Ownership Who creates and owns each handler and driver 7 MotorController The heart of the board: the TMC9660 motor controller 8 The other managers Encoders, IMU, ADC, temperature, GPIO, LED, comms and NVS 9 Threading and errors What is safe to call from several tasks, and how failures are reported 10 Examples Which app to run to see each feature

When you change code, Testing and CI says what CI will check, and Decisions explains why the code is shaped the way it is.

docs.title: Managers
docs.text:
A manager is the one object that owns a board function: it knows which chips and pins implement it (from the pin map), creates and owns the hf-core handlers for them, and gives you a small API. Every manager is a singleton reached through the Vortex facade.

Manager Member What it gives you Start-up step CommChannelsManager vortex.comms SPI2 devices, the I2C bus, the UART to the TMC9660, the TWAI (CAN) bus required NvsManager vortex.nvs Three flash key-value namespaces: application, calibration, configuration required GpioManager vortex.gpio Every GPIO-category pin by name or enum, on the ESP32-C6, the PCAL95555 and the TMC9660 required MotorController vortex.motors The onboard TMC9660 (and up to two external ones), motor and load-frame velocity and position best effort AdcManager vortex.adc The 15 TMC9660-hosted ADC channels: currents, supply voltages, temperatures, AIN inputs best effort ImuManager vortex.imu The onboard BNO08x IMU and up to three external ones, data-ready interrupts best effort EncoderManager vortex.encoders Up to four AS5047U angle encoders, created by you best effort LedManager vortex.leds The WS2812 status LED: colours, brightness, animations, status patterns required TemperatureManager vortex.temp ESP32-C6 die, NTC thermistor and TMC9660 chip temperatures best effort

Every manager has the same lifecycle calls: GetInstance(), EnsureInitialized() (idempotent), IsInitialized(), Deinitialize() (or Shutdown() for the LED manager), GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(...) and DumpStatistics(). The start-up step column says whether a failure stops Vortex::EnsureInitialized(); see Initialisation.

docs.title: AdcManager
docs.text: Gives you every ADC channel of the pin map by name or by enum. On Vortex V1 all of them are hosted by the TMC9660: its analog inputs AIN0 to AIN3 and its internal measurements (phase currents, supply and driver voltages, chip and external temperatures, motor current, velocity and position). The ESP32-C6's own ADC is not used. Source: AdcManager.h.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text: The channels and their names are in the pin map. Every one is read through a single Tmc9660AdcWrapper that borrows the onboard TMC9660 handler from MotorController, so this manager is up only if the motor controller is.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Call Notes ReadVoltage(name, float& volts, samples = 1, time_between_samples = 0) Also takes an HfFunctionalAdcChannel; averages samples readings ReadRaw(name, uint32_t& raw, samples = 1, time_between_samples = 0) Raw counts; also takes the enum Get(name), Get(HfFunctionalAdcChannel) BaseAdc* for the channel, or nullptr Contains(name), Size() Lookup helpers GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(AdcSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Counters and the last error

docs.title: Example: read the supply voltage
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/AdcManager.h"

auto& adc = Vortex::GetInstance().adc;
float vsupply = 0.0f;
if (adc.ReadVoltage(HfFunctionalAdcChannel::TMC9660_SUPPLY_VOLTAGE, vsupply, 4) == hf_adc_err_t::ADC_SUCCESS) {
    // vsupply holds the average of four readings
}

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Depends on the TMC9660. If MotorController did not start, every read fails; check adc.IsInitialized().
  • Internal channels are TMC9660 parameters, read over the motor controller's host link (UART or SPI), so a read costs a TMCL transaction, not a microsecond ADC conversion.
  • Use names from the pin map (or the enum). A name that is not in the map returns an error, not a reading.

docs.title: CommChannelsManager
docs.text: Owns every bus on the board and hands out device handles. Other managers get their buses from it; your code normally needs it only to talk to an external SPI or I2C device, or to the CAN bus. Source: CommChannelsManager.h.

docs.title: The buses
docs.text:
Bus Settings at start-up Devices SPI2 10 MHz per device by default TMC9660_MOTOR_CONTROLLER (mode 3), AS5047U_POSITION_ENCODER (mode 1), EXTERNAL_DEVICE_1 and EXTERNAL_DEVICE_2 (mode 0) I2C 100 kHz for the built-in devices BNO08x IMU at 0x4A, PCAL95555 at 0x20, plus a bounded number of devices you add at run time UART 115200 baud TMCL link to the TMC9660 TWAI (CAN) 500 kbit/s The CAN port; GetCanOpenBus() is an alias of GetCanBus() for CANopen code

Pins are in the pin map (the COMM_* rows).

docs.title: API
docs.text: Call Notes GetSpiDevice(SpiDeviceId), GetSpiDevice(uint8_t index) BaseSpi* for one chip select, or nullptr GetI2cDevice(I2cDeviceId), GetI2cDevice(bus_index, device_index) BaseI2c* for a built-in or runtime device CreateI2cDevice(address, speed_hz = 400000) Adds a runtime I2C device; returns its index, or -1 on failure RemoveI2cDevice(index), I2cProbeAddress(address, timeout_ms), I2cScanBus(out, max), I2cResetBus() Runtime I2C helpers GetUartBus() BaseUart* to the TMC9660 link GetCanBus(), GetCanOpenBus() BaseCan* GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(CommSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Per-bus validity, device counts, last error

docs.title: Example: scan the I2C bus
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/CommChannelsManager.h"

auto& comms = Vortex::GetInstance().comms;
uint8_t found[16] = {};
const size_t n = comms.I2cScanBus(found, sizeof(found));
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    ESP_LOGI("app", "I2C device at 0x%02X", found[i]);   // expect 0x20 (PCAL95555) and 0x4A (BNO08x)
}

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: GetSystemDiagnostics() fills CommSystemDiagnostics: whether SPI, I2C, UART and CAN are valid, the number of SPI devices and runtime I2C devices, and the last error. DumpStatistics() logs the same.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Borrowed pointers. The returned bus pointers belong to the manager; do not delete them and do not keep them across Deinitialize().
  • The accessors and the runtime I2C calls take no lock. Add devices during start-up, from one task. See Threading.
  • SPI2 and the TMC9660 mux. The TMC9660 sees SPI2 only while PCAL_TMC_SPI_COMM_EN selects it. MotorController handles this for its own transfers; do not drive that pin yourself.
  • Runtime I2C devices are heap-allocated, so create them at start-up, not in a control loop.

docs.title: EncoderManager
docs.text: Owns up to four AS5047U magnetic angle encoders. Vortex V1 has a chip select wired for one encoder (AS5047U_POSITION_ENCODER, GPIO20) and two external chip selects that can each take another, but no encoder is created automatically: you create each device. Source: EncoderManager.h.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Call Notes CreateAs5047uDevice(index, SpiDeviceId, config = default) Creates an encoder on one of the board's chip selects; also an overload taking a BaseSpi& DeleteDevice(index) Removes it ReadAngle(index, uint16_t& counts), ReadAngleDegrees(index, double& deg) 14-bit angle, or degrees ReadVelocityRPM(index, double& rpm) Velocity from the sensor ReadDiagnostics(index, As5047uDiagnostics&), SetZeroPosition(index, counts) Sensor diagnostics, zero offset ReadAllAngles(...), ReadAllVelocities(...), CheckAllDevicesHealth() Every active device, under the manager lock GetAs5047uHandler(index), GetAs5047uDriver(index) The handler or the typed driver for chip features IsDeviceValid, GetActiveDeviceIndices, GetAvailableDevices, GetDeviceType Device bookkeeping GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(EncoderSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Counters and the last error

docs.title: Example: create the onboard-slot encoder and read it
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/EncoderManager.h"

auto& enc = Vortex::GetInstance().encoders;
if (enc.CreateAs5047uDevice(0, SpiDeviceId::AS5047U_POSITION_ENCODER)) {
    double deg = 0.0;
    if (enc.ReadAngleDegrees(0, deg) == EncoderError::SUCCESS) {
        // deg is the shaft angle, 0 to 360
    }
}

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Nothing to read until you create a device. EnsureInitialized() succeeds with zero devices.
  • SPI2 is shared with the TMC9660 (when on SPI) and the external slots.
  • Single-device reads take no manager lock. Read one encoder from one task, or use ReadAllAngles(). See Threading.
  • The TMC9660 can use the same encoder. The position benches feed the AS5047U angle to the host while the TMC9660 uses its own ABN input; decide which side owns the feedback before you close a loop on it.

docs.title: GpioManager
docs.text: Registers every GPIO-category pin of the pin map, whichever chip it is on, and lets you drive or read it by name or by enum. On Vortex V1 those pins live on three chips: the ESP32-C6, the PCAL95555 I/O expander and the TMC9660. Source: GpioManager.h.

docs.title: Which pins it owns
docs.text:
At start-up it walks the pin map and registers the pins whose category is GPIO (and the user, ADC and SPI categories). Core pins (crystal, boot, USB) and comm pins (bus lines, the LED data line) are skipped; their owners configure them. The names are the Name column of the pin map, for example GPIO_PCAL_TMC_DRV_EN, GPIO_PCAL_IMU_RST, GPIO_EXT_GPIO_CS_1.

Chip Pins How they are reached ESP32-C6 The two external chip selects An EspGpio the manager creates PCAL95555 TMC9660 control and fault lines, IMU boot / interrupt / reset, CAN standby, power good, TMC9660 GPIO17/18 read-back Pin objects from the Pcal95555Handler, over I2C TMC9660 TMC_GPIO17, TMC_GPIO18 The TMC9660 handler, registered once MotorController has created the onboard device

Each pin takes its polarity from the pin map. "Active" means the asserted level, so for an active-low pin SetActive() drives it low.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Call Notes Get(std::string_view name), Get(HfFunctionalGpioPin pin) std::shared_ptr<BaseGpio>, empty if the pin is not registered Set(name, bool active), SetActive(name), SetInactive(name), Toggle(name) Return hf_gpio_err_t Read(name, bool& active), IsActive(name, bool& active) Logical state: true means asserted (polarity applied) SetDirection, SetPullMode, SetOutputMode Reconfigure a pin at run time ConfigureInterrupt(...), EnableInterrupt, DisableInterrupt, SupportsInterrupts Edge interrupts on pins that support them Contains(name), Size() Lookup helpers GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(GpioSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Operation counters and the last error

docs.title: Example: read the TMC9660 fault line
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/GpioManager.h"

auto& gpio = Vortex::GetInstance().gpio;
bool fault = false;
if (gpio.Read("GPIO_PCAL_TMC_FAULT_STATUS", fault) == hf_gpio_err_t::GPIO_SUCCESS && fault) {
    // the TMC9660 is signalling a fault (the line is active low; Read() reports "asserted")
}

In a loop, look the pin up once and keep it: auto drv = gpio.Get(HfFunctionalGpioPin::PCAL_TMC_DRV_EN);. The string calls search the table on every call.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: GetSystemDiagnostics() reports the number of registered pins and the total, successful and failed operation counts. DumpStatistics() logs the same, with per-pin access and error counts.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Read() returns the logical state, not the electrical level: the header comment says "true = high", but the code returns IsActive(). For an active-low pin, true means the line is low.
  • Expander pins are slow. Every PCAL95555 access is an I2C transfer; do not toggle them in a fast loop.
  • MotorController owns the TMC9660 control lines. Driving PCAL_TMC_DRV_EN, PCAL_TMC_RST_CTRL or PCAL_TMC_SPI_COMM_EN yourself disables or confuses the motor controller.
  • No lock on pin operations. Give each pin one owner task. See Threading.
  • A wrong name returns GPIO_ERR_PIN_NOT_FOUND. Copy names from the pin map.

docs.title: ImuManager
docs.text: Owns the BNO08x IMUs: the onboard one on I2C at 0x4A, and up to three external ones on I2C or SPI. The BNO08x runs its own sensor fusion; this manager creates its handler (which drives the reset and boot lines on the PCAL95555) and optionally wires its data-ready interrupt. Source: ImuManager.h.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: Index Device Created by 0 Onboard BNO08x (I2C 0x4A) ImuManager::EnsureInitialized() 1 to 3 External BNO08x You: CreateExternalBno08xDevice(index, i2c_address, speed_hz) or CreateExternalBno08xDevice(index, SpiDeviceId)

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Call Notes GetBno08xHandler(index = 0) Bno08xHandler*, or nullptr GetSensor(index = 0) IBno08xDriverOps*: the driver itself (enable reports, read the latest data) CreateExternalBno08xDevice(...), DeleteExternalDevice(index) External IMUs ConfigureInterrupt(index, callback), EnableInterrupt, DisableInterrupt, IsInterruptEnabled, WaitForInterrupt(index, timeout_ms) Data-ready interrupt; the onboard IMU uses PCAL_IMU_INT through GpioManager IsDeviceValid, GetActiveDeviceIndices, GetAvailableDevices, GetDeviceType Device bookkeeping GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(ImuSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Health per device

On the handler, Update() services the SH-2 protocol and dispatches new reports to the callback set with SetSensorCallback(); visitDriver() runs a function on the driver under the handler's lock.

docs.title: Example: poll the onboard IMU
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/ImuManager.h"

auto& imu = Vortex::GetInstance().imu;
if (Bno08xHandler* h = imu.GetBno08xHandler(); h != nullptr) {
    // Set a callback once with h->SetSensorCallback(...), then service the device periodically:
    (void)h->Update();
}

The bench app vortex_pcal_gpio_imu_bringup and the manager test encoder_imu_test in Examples show reports being enabled and read.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: GetSystemDiagnostics() fills ImuSystemDiagnostics: whether the manager is up, active and initialised device counts, the last error, and a snapshot per device.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• The IMU's control lines are on the expander. Reset, boot and interrupt go through the PCAL95555 over I2C, so GpioManager must be up first (the facade orders this).
  • Call Update() often enough. The BNO08x queues reports; if nothing services it, reports are dropped.
  • I2C is shared with the PCAL95555. Long I2C transactions from your code delay IMU servicing.

docs.title: LedManager
docs.text: Drives the single WS2812 RGB status LED (data on GPIO3, through the ESP32-C6's RMT peripheral): solid colours, brightness, simple animations and a set of system status patterns. It starts early (step 4) so an LED-only bench works without the motor controller. Source: LedManager.h.

docs.text: Call Notes SetColor(LedColor), SetColor(uint32_t rgb), TurnOff(), GetCurrentColor(LedColor&) LedColors::RED, GREEN, BLUE, YELLOW, CYAN, MAGENTA, WHITE, ORANGE, PURPLE, BLACK SetBrightnessPercent(0..100), SetBrightnessRaw(0..255), SetMaxBrightness(...) Brightness, capped by the maximum StartAnimation(LedAnimation, colour), StopAnimation(), UpdateAnimation(), IsAnimationActive() SOLID, BLINK, BREATH, RAINBOW and the status patterns IndicateBoot(), IndicateReady(), IndicateWarning(), IndicateError(), IndicateCalibration() Blue blink, solid green, yellow blink, red fast blink, cyan breathe GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(LedSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Counters and the last error

docs.title: Example: show the start-up result
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/LedManager.h"

auto& vortex = Vortex::GetInstance();
const bool ok = vortex.EnsureInitialized();
if (vortex.leds.IsInitialized()) {
    (void)(ok ? vortex.leds.IndicateReady() : vortex.leds.IndicateError());
}
// in a periodic task, about every 50 ms:
//   (void)vortex.leds.UpdateAnimation();

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Animations need a caller. The manager has no task; blink, breath, rainbow and the blinking status patterns move only when you call UpdateAnimation() (the step is 50 ms).
  • It is a required start-up step. If the RMT channel cannot be set up, Vortex::EnsureInitialized() fails.
  • Full white at full brightness is bright and draws current. Use SetMaxBrightness() to cap it.

docs.title: MotorController
docs.text: Owns the TMC9660 motor controllers: the onboard one, and up to two more on the external SPI chip selects. The TMC9660 runs the motor loops itself (FOC current, velocity and position, ramps); this manager creates its handler, manages the host link and gives you unit-aware velocity and position calls in the motor frame or, through a gear ratio, the load frame. Source: MotorController.h.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text:
Index Device Created by 0 Onboard TMC9660 Vortex::EnsureInitialized() (start-up step 5), on UART by default or SPI if selected 2, 3 External TMC9660 on EXTERNAL_DEVICE_1 / EXTERNAL_DEVICE_2 You: CreateExternalDevice()

The onboard device needs the four control lines on the PCAL95555 (reset, driver enable, fault, wake), which the facade takes from GpioManager. The transport is chosen with Vortex::SetOnboardTmc9660Transport() before initialisation; see Initialisation.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Call Notes handler(index = 0) Tmc9660Handler*, or nullptr if there is no device at that index visitDriver(func, index = 0) Calls func(auto& driver) with the typed TMC9660 driver (SPI or UART variant); the way to reach every TMCL parameter setMotorVelocity / getMotorVelocity, setMotorPosition / getMotorPosition Motor (rotor) frame; take a value, a tmc9660::units unit and a MotorContext setMotorMechanics(MotorMechanics), getMotorMechanics() Gear ratio (motor turns per output turn) and output inversion setLoadVelocity / getLoadVelocity, setLoadPosition / getLoadPosition Load (output shaft) frame, through the mechanics CreateExternalDevice(cs_index, ...), DeleteExternalDevice(cs_index) External TMC9660 over SPI or UART IsDeviceValid, GetActiveDeviceIndices, InitializeAllDevices, GetInitializationStatus Device bookkeeping GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(MotorSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Health per device

A MotorContext tells the unit conversions about the motor: motor type, pole pairs, velocity sensor and encoder counts per revolution.

docs.title: Example: run the load shaft at 30 rpm
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/MotorController.h"

using ::tmc9660::units::VelocityUnit;

constexpr ::tmc9660::units::MotorContext kCtx{
    tmc9660::tmcl::MotorType::BLDC_MOTOR,
    7,                                                  // pole pairs of your motor
    tmc9660::tmcl::VelocitySensorSelection::DIGITAL_HALL,
    0u,                                                 // encoder counts per revolution (none)
};

auto& motors = Vortex::GetInstance().motors;
if (motors.IsInitialized() && motors.handler() != nullptr) {
    (void)motors.setMotorMechanics(MotorMechanics{10.0, false});   // 10:1 reducer
    (void)motors.setLoadVelocity(30.0, VelocityUnit::Rpm, kCtx);
}

Commanding motion assumes the TMC9660 has been configured for your motor (type, pole pairs, current limits, feedback, commutation mode). The BLDC bring-up notes and the motor bench examples (vortex_bldc_* in Examples) show the full sequence.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: GetSystemDiagnostics() fills MotorSystemDiagnostics: whether the manager is up, how many device slots are active and initialised, the last error, and per device whether it is active, initialised and its error count.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• No motor manager, no TMC9660 features. If the onboard TMC9660 does not come up (for example with its supply off), step 5 fails with a warning. Everything that depends on the TMC9660 (ADC channels, the NTC and chip temperatures, TMC_GPIO17/18) is then unavailable too.
  • Pick the transport before start-up. SetOnboardTmc9660Transport() after EnsureInitialized() is ignored.
  • The SPI mux is shared. On SPI, MotorController asserts PCAL_TMC_SPI_COMM_EN around its transfers; other SPI2 users must not assume the TMC9660 is off the bus.
  • Index 1 is not a device. External devices use the chip-select indices 2 and 3.
  • Do not copy evaluation-kit pin numbers. Hall and ABN wiring on Vortex need not match the TMC9660 kit; use the pin map and the bring-up notes.

docs.title: NvsManager
docs.text: Persistent key-value storage in the ESP32-C6's flash (ESP-IDF NVS), split into three namespaces and exposed as the board-independent BaseNvs interface. It starts first, so calibration and configuration can be read before the buses come up. Source: NvsManager.h.

docs.title: The namespaces
docs.text:
Accessor NVS namespace Use it for App() vortex General application keys Calibration() vortex_cal Calibration and factory tuning blobs Config() vortex_cfg Structured device configuration

Each returns a BaseNvs&. Code written against BaseNvs keeps working if the storage moves to another medium.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Call Notes App(), Calibration(), Config() BaseNvs& for one namespace On a BaseNvs: SetU32 / GetU32, SetString, SetBlob, GetSize, KeyExists, EraseKey, Commit Return hf_nvs_err_t (except KeyExists) GetLastError() Set when initialisation fails DumpStatistics() Logs each namespace

docs.title: Example: count boots
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/NvsManager.h"

BaseNvs& app = Vortex::GetInstance().nvs.App();
hf_u32_t boots = 0;
(void)app.GetU32("boots", boots);           // stays 0 if the key does not exist yet
if (app.SetU32("boots", boots + 1) == hf_nvs_err_t::NVS_SUCCESS) {
    (void)app.Commit();
}

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Commit. Writes are not guaranteed to reach flash until Commit().
  • Key length. ESP-IDF limits keys to 15 characters (GetMaxKeyLength()).
  • No lock in the manager. Initialise it once (the facade does); concurrent access to one namespace relies on ESP-IDF NVS itself.

docs.title: TemperatureManager
docs.text: Reads the board's three temperature sources by name and gives simple statistics across them. It is up if at least one sensor works. Source: TemperatureManager.h.

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text: Name Source Needs ESP32_INTERNAL The ESP32-C6's on-chip sensor (die temperature) nothing NTC_THERMISTOR NTC thermistor on TMC9660 input AIN3, through AdcManager (ADC_TMC9660_AIN3) AdcManager, so the TMC9660 MOTOR_TEMP The TMC9660's internal chip temperature MotorController

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Call Notes ReadTemperatureCelsius(name, float&), ReadTemperatureFahrenheit(name, float&) By sensor name ReadInternalTemperature(float&), ReadNtcTemperature(float&), ReadMotorTemperature(float&) Shortcuts for the three names GetSystemTemperatureStats(min, max, avg) Across the registered sensors GetSensorCount(), GetSensorEntry(name) Registered sensors GetLastError(), GetSystemDiagnostics(TempSystemDiagnostics&), DumpStatistics() Counters and the last error

All reads return hf_temp_err_t; TEMP_SUCCESS is 0.

docs.title: Example: board and chip temperature
docs.text:
#include "api/Vortex.h"
#include "managers/TemperatureManager.h"

auto& temp = Vortex::GetInstance().temp;
float board_c = 0.0f, chip_c = 0.0f;
const bool have_board = temp.ReadNtcTemperature(board_c) == hf_temp_err_t::TEMP_SUCCESS;
const bool have_chip = temp.ReadMotorTemperature(chip_c) == hf_temp_err_t::TEMP_SUCCESS;

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Two of three sensors depend on the TMC9660. Without the motor controller only ESP32_INTERNAL reads.
  • The die temperature is not the board temperature. It runs above ambient with the CPU load.
  • MOTOR_TEMP is the controller chip, not the motor winding.
